headline: High-risk pair: Gemini CLI can write/egress from shared files while RD-Agent uploads to third-party APIs, creating default data-leakage and cascading-error exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Gemini CLI can read/write repo files and use MCP, while RD-Agent can consume files/logs and run browser/API workflows. A shared filesystem or copied outputs create a plausible instruction-injection bridge, but no direct shared channel is documented. Uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or log directory, THEN file content from one can influence the other.
IF Gemini CLI is allowed to read untrusted files that RD-Agent later parses, THEN prompt injection becomes feasible.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Disable MCP for untrusted directories.
Review any file passed between agents before reuse.
Use read-only mounts for shared inputs.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Gemini CLI has broad network egress and reads user files; RD-Agent sends data to OpenAI/Azure/DeepSeek/LiteLLM and handles logs plus sensitive research/financial datasets. If they share files or credentials, Gemini content can reach third-party APIs through RD-Agent, making leakage plausible in default-style workflows.
conditions: IF the same directory contains secrets, datasets, or reports for both agents, THEN either agent can expose them through its outbound APIs.
IF Gemini CLI writes artifacts that RD-Agent ingests, THEN those artifacts can be transmitted to third-party model providers.
mitigations: Use separate directories and credentials.
Remove secrets from shared paths.
Disable outbound API calls for sensitive runs.
Restrict RD-Agent to sanitized inputs only.
requires-engineering: enforce data-loss-prevention controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Gemini CLI can modify git state and write the filesystem; RD-Agent writes logs and uses Docker-based isolation. They can contend over shared repo files or git state if co-located, but RD-Agent does not advertise unrestricted filesystem writes, so the strongest conflict indicator is not met.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same git checkout, THEN concurrent edits can overwrite each other.
IF RD-Agent writes logs into a directory Gemini CLI also edits, THEN file races can occur.
mitigations: Run each agent in its own checkout.
Serialize git operations.
Make log directories append-only.
Use file locks for shared artifacts.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Gemini CLI can generate code and shell actions, and RD-Agent is an automation/research system that can act on model outputs and APIs. If RD-Agent treats Gemini-produced artifacts as authoritative, errors can cascade into API calls, commits, or bad research outputs. The interaction is inferred, but the blast radius is broad.
conditions: IF RD-Agent consumes Gemini CLI output without verification, THEN incorrect facts can propagate into downstream actions.
IF Gemini CLI produces code or commands that RD-Agent executes, THEN a single mistake can affect multiple work products.
mitigations: Require human review before execution.
Add schema validation on exchanged outputs.
Use a second model or rule-based checker.
Limit RD-Agent to read-only analysis mode.
requires-engineering: implement provenance and approval gates.

E_compliance.rationale: Gemini CLI can touch local files and shell environment, while RD-Agent handles financial reports, research datasets, logs, and sends data to third-party APIs. That creates a plausible compliance breach path for sensitive data residency or retention, especially if regulated data is placed in shared files. No documented cross-agent compliance controls are provided.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared workspace, THEN both agents may process it under different retention and transfer rules.
IF EU or confidential data is routed through RD-Agent APIs, THEN residency or DPA requirements may be violated.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared folders.
Use region-approved API endpoints only.
Purge logs after each run.
Separate credentials by jurisdiction.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data residency and retention.
